name: ARTEX
origin: Open-source, Go, published on GitHub by "Autumn-27" in July 2026; made unavailable on 2026-10-08, with forks, archived copies and a commercial ARTEX PRO still in circulation
models: External providers (Claude, GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, Kimi); DeepSeek Flash models dominate attacker instances per the FBI
summary: Multi-agent, LLM-driven penetration-testing platform: an operator sets a target and objective, a planner agent chooses steps and worker agents run standard tools, sharing findings. Reported in use by state-aligned and financially motivated actors since August 2026; its own consoles are often exposed to the internet. Spectrum's census (2026-11-18) counted 2,335 exposed offensive AI consoles, 47 distinct ARTEX variants (forks, private builds, renamed consoles such as ScopeWeaver) and 179 ARTEX consoles that a default-title search misses.

name: AntiFox
origin: Open-source fork of ARTEX 0.1.1, maintained under the AntiFox-AI GitHub organisation
summary: Self-hosted, Chinese-language agentic pentest platform whose README calls it secondary development of ARTEX; tied by Arctic Wolf Labs (as read by the Cloud Security Alliance) to IIS and AWS intrusions.

name: PentAGI
summary: Autonomous offensive framework aimed at lowering the barrier for entry-level operators; GTIG observed a customised orchestration platform built on it in the wild.

name: CAIRN
summary: Open-source multi-agent pentest framework built on an observe-orient-decide-act loop in which specialised agents share a blackboard; given a target and a plain-language goal it runs for hours on its own. Seen in the wild by GTIG, by Gambit (financially motivated retail-skimming operator) and by Amazon Threat Intelligence (Chinese-nexus operator whose Cairn agents found and exploited a MONAI Label zero-day).

name: CyberStrikeAI
origin: Open-source, Go backend acting as C2 and orchestration server
summary: Open-source Go platform whose control server uses an LLM to pick tools while a plain implant executes them; besides GTIG's experimentation reporting, it is now documented in intrusions at education organisations in Africa and Latin America (Kaspersky), an AWS intrusion (Elastic) and attempts against Japanese organisations (JPCERT/CC).

name: HexStrike AI
summary: MCP-integrated harness that lets LLM clients drive a large set of pre-installed offensive security tools; GTIG reports experimentation by threat actors and one PRC-nexus intrusion using it with a memory system.

name: Strix
summary: Multi-agent framework for automated vulnerability identification and validation, seen in a PRC-nexus intrusion (GTIG) and in a financially motivated card-skimming operation (Gambit).

name: ScopeSentry
origin: Open-source asset-mapping and scanning platform (FastAPI server, Go scan nodes, Vue UI) by Autumn-27, the GitHub handle that also published ARTEX; AGPL-3.0 with separate commercial terms; upstream since June 2024. The niudaii fork (v1.9.4, 2026-08-26) adds an ARTEX task client and an MCP server
models: None of its own. In the fork, an asset can be sent to an ARTEX instance as a scan task, and the MCP server lets an AI client (for example Cursor) list assets and create scans with an API key
summary: Distributed recon platform: subdomains, ports, fingerprints, directory and vulnerability scans, leaks, crawling and page monitoring across scan nodes. Not malicious in itself. It matters here because the fork wires reconnaissance to agentic exploitation: the asset view has a 'scan task' action that logs into an ARTEX API (default port 8787, user 'ARTEX') and posts the asset as the task goal, and the configuration ships a default ARTEX address on a public IP. Sharing a GitHub handle with ARTEX's author is not evidence that the author is behind any intrusion.

name: Hermes Agent
origin: Open-source (MIT) general-purpose persistent agent by Nous Research, with an unattended (YOLO) mode
summary: Legitimate agent with ordinary users, abused in intrusions: run with approvals off against Thailand's Ministry of Finance (Hunt.io), installed by the Carbonato botnet as a Telegram-controlled interface that hunts AI API keys (ThreatDown), and found on a retail card-theft operator's staging server (Gambit). Hunt the abuse signature, not the agent.
